stories.headline: Zest launches AI agent that finds restaurants and books tables via text
stories.dek: The startup moves its recommendation engine from app to SMS, letting groups coordinate dining choices and reserve through one conversation thread.
stories.summary:
Zest, a restaurant-discovery app launched in late 2024 that uses credit card transaction history to personalize recommendations, has released a text-based AI concierge accessible at a dedicated number. Users can request restaurant suggestions filtered by cuisine, occasion, dietary needs, or location; ask operational questions like WiFi availability or current crowding; and request menus—all within SMS. The agent integrates with reservation platforms (OpenTable, Resy, SevenRooms) to check real-time availability and book tables without leaving the conversation thread.

The shift reflects a deliberate bet that conversational interfaces will displace dedicated mobile apps for certain tasks. In group chats, the concierge blends all participants' dining histories to find consensus options and can facilitate in-thread voting before booking for the entire party. Zest founder Mario Gomez-Hall frames this as moving from app-first to agent-first product design, arguing that the concierge learns user preferences faster than general assistants because it anchors recommendations in actual transaction history rather than survey responses.

Zest began private testing in September and launched publicly after adding booking capabilities. The company sees booking and food ordering as near-term revenue streams and views the taste model—built on real spending data—as defensible beyond dining, with longer-term ambitions to cover shopping, entertainment, and other discovery use cases.
stories.why_it_matters: For your consultancy, this is a production-grade example of an AI agent handling sequential, multi-modal tasks: parsing user intent across a group, querying external data sources, coordinating with third-party APIs, and executing transactions—all within a stateless conversational medium. It demonstrates how binding an agent to real transaction data (rather than surveys or conversation history) accelerates personalization and trustworthiness. For L&D, it's a concrete architecture to deconstruct in workshops: how agents route requests, maintain context in group scenarios, and automate hand-offs to booking systems.
stories.potential_use: Use this as a workshop case study: walk through the decision tree Zest's agent likely implements (parsing party size, cuisine filters, time constraints, then checking availability, then collecting votes, then calling reservation APIs). Discuss with clients how their customer-facing workflows map to similar multi-step agent patterns. Also consider: how does Zest's use of transaction history as a foundation data layer differ from pure LLM-based recommendation systems, and what does that mean for building defensible AI products?

sources.title: Zest’s new AI agent finds restaurants and books reservations over text

stories.headline: Big Tech's AI spending surge hits a cash flow wall
stories.dek: Alphabet, Amazon, and Meta report negative free cash flow as $740B capex bets fail to convert to returns investors expected.
stories.summary:
Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft have collectively committed over $740 billion to AI infrastructure this year—data centers, chips, compute—betting on explosive returns. But the market reaction this week signals that investors' patience is wearing thin. Alphabet fell 12% Thursday (its worst day on record) after reporting negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion in Q3, with capex hitting $51.4 billion. Amazon swung to negative $42.4 billion free cash flow over the past 12 months and dropped 7% after earnings. Meta reported negative $2.1 billion free cash flow in Q3 despite 26% ad revenue growth. Only Microsoft posted positive free cash flow of $18.6 billion, though it blamed delays from third-party providers for spending less than planned.

The core problem: these companies' cash-generation engines are straining under AI's weight. Google's Search business—which generates roughly half the company's revenue—saw advertising growth slow to 12%, its weakest pace in five quarters, as AI features like Mode cannibalize search monetization. Amazon's cloud business grew 39% but didn't offset capex burden. Meta's new AI agent Muse is "very compute-intensive to run," according to CEO Mark Zuckerberg.

The financing picture reveals the scale of the wager. The five major tech firms raised a combined $326 billion in debt in 2026, triple the amount from 2025. Smaller companies renting AI compute saw share prices sink on Microsoft's capex shortfall signals. The uncertainty now threatens downstream ventures: Anthropic's highly anticipated IPO filing this week faces headwinds as Blackstone warned investors the AI startup might not achieve investment-grade credit ratings post-launch, potentially forcing greater dependence on hyperscalers for infrastructure funding.
stories.why_it_matters: For your consultancy and workshops, this exposes the hard economic reality behind AI hype: massive infrastructure spending doesn't automatically translate to profitability or defensible business models. Understanding the cash flow math and ROI pressure will sharpen how you advise clients on which AI applications genuinely create moat versus which are cash-burning capacity grabs. It also signals that the willingness to absorb losses for growth is finite—investors are pivoting from "spend to win" to "where's the return," which will reshape which AI bets actually get funded and which applications will survive the efficiency reckoning ahead.
stories.potential_use: Use this as a teaching case in workshops: walk through the waterfall from capex → operational cash → free cash flow to show students and clients how AI infrastructure bets stress balance sheets even at scale. Frame for your consultancy as a positioning angle: help enterprise clients avoid the same trap by building realistic unit economics and monetization *before* scaling compute spend, not after. Track how Indian AI firms navigate this dynamic—domestic startups and enterprises may learn from or diverge from hyperscaler patterns depending on access to capital and customer demand.

sources.title: Cracks are emerging in the AI spending boom

stories.headline: DoorDash reports only hundreds of AI agent orders despite commerce automation hype
stories.dek: The delivery platform received several hundred autonomous orders against 3 million daily human orders, illustrating the gap between agent adoption expectations and current reality.
stories.summary:
DoorDash disclosed in its third-quarter earnings that autonomous AI agents have placed only several hundred orders on its platform, a figure trivial against its 3 million daily completions. Agents from providers like Muse, Instinct, and Fo represent a nascent but not yet significant commerce channel. CEO Tony Xu framed the moment carefully—avoiding both dismissiveness and false optimism—noting that the company wants to understand agentic use cases without being "delusional" about current traction.

The company has built its own agent portfolio: a text-to-order agent (September), a CLI tool (July), Ask DoorDash chatbot (June), and an MCP standard for corporate ordering through third-party chatbots. Meanwhile, the ecosystem remains fragmented. Amazon blocks personal agents from its site; Walmart actively welcomes them to capture competitor traffic.

The data underscores a recurring pattern in AI adoption: early products and bold predictions outpace genuine user behavior. For delivery platforms and merchants, this means agent integration is infrastructure-building for a future that remains distant, not an immediate channel shift.
stories.why_it_matters: This provides concrete evidence for recalibrating AI agent adoption timelines and capability assumptions—essential for your consulting work around realistic implementation roadmaps. The numbers demolish inflated narratives about autonomous purchasing, offering a teaching anchor for workshops on the difference between technical feasibility and market adoption. It also signals that platforms are hedging: building agent infrastructure while platform-native experiences (apps, chatbots) remain dominant, a strategic posture worth understanding for clients planning agent strategies.
stories.potential_use: Use this in workshops to ground discussions on AI adoption curves and inflated expectations—have participants estimate agent order volume before revealing the actual number, then discuss why reality lags hype. For consulting: this is a talking point when clients pitch agent-first commerce strategies; anchor them to DoorDash's own evidence. Relevant for India ecosystem tracking: how are Indian delivery platforms (Zomato, Swiggy) approaching agents, and are they seeing similar adoption patterns or different market dynamics?

sources.title: DoorDash said it’s only received ‘several hundred’ orders from AI agents

stories.headline: Runware plans to mass-produce AI data centers at 30MW per day by 2028
stories.dek: The Romanian startup is setting up a second factory to build modular pods on an assembly line, aiming to cut deployment time to 48 hours.
stories.summary:
Runware is shifting from custom-building data centers to factory-based manufacturing. The company operates one existing factory and is completing a second one expected to come online in early 2027. By 2028, Runware aims to produce 30 megawatts of capacity daily—roughly equivalent to the entire U.S. data center buildout projected for a single year. Each pod ships ready to install and can go live within 48 hours of arrival at a customer site; build time per unit is dropping from three weeks to one day as production scales.

The startup has already received $1 billion in committed interest for its Sonic Inference Pods since opening orders a month ago. Runware says it can keep costs competitive by designing its own cooling and support systems using standard, off-the-shelf components, though it still depends on Nvidia for networking hardware. The company has recruited an automotive industry veteran as plant manager to handle execution—a deliberate move to avoid the manufacturing pitfalls that sank EV startup Arrival.

Runware has raised $60 million to date and plans a Series B; the current factory build is being financed from its $50 million Series A. The company is working with power providers on a pipeline covering 397 megawatts initially, targeting smaller sites than hyperscalers typically use and prioritizing renewable energy sources. It intends to expand production first to other regions worldwide after launching the second factory.
stories.why_it_matters: For an AI consultant building practical expertise: this represents a real-time test of whether infrastructure economics can be fundamentally reshaped. If Runware executes at scale, it removes a major deployment bottleneck for enterprise AI applications—not just the ability to get compute, but to provision it in months rather than years. For your workshop teaching, it's a concrete example of how infrastructure innovation changes what becomes feasible to build. For tracking India's ecosystem, watch whether Runware or competitors target India's growing data center demand or whether local players emerge with similar mass-production approaches.
stories.potential_use: Workshop demo: compare the unit economics Runware claims (standardized manufacturing + shorter deployment cycles) against traditional data center capex to illustrate how infrastructure constraints translate to application constraints. For consulting: begin horizon-scanning which enterprise clients could unlock new AI use cases if hardware provisioning moved from 12-18 months to weeks—sectors with seasonal demand or ad-hoc compute needs are the early targets. India angle: monitor whether Indian AI startups or cloud providers license Runware's modular design or build competing approaches.

sources.title: Can AI data centers be mass-produced like cars? This startup aims to find out

stories.headline: OpenAI adopts robots.txt signal for AI training opt-outs
stories.dek: Website owners can now use a standard robots.txt directive to signal they don't want their content used to train AI models.
stories.summary:
OpenAI has committed to respecting a shared robots.txt signal that lets website operators communicate their preferences about AI model training to participating providers. Rather than building proprietary opt-out mechanisms, OpenAI is adopting an established web standard—the robots.txt protocol originally designed for search engine crawlers—to handle AI training preferences.

The move addresses a growing friction point between AI companies and content creators. Website owners now have a standardized, machine-readable way to express that their content should not be used for training, rather than having to navigate different policies and request processes across multiple AI providers. By relying on robots.txt, sites can manage their AI training preferences alongside existing crawler directives in a single, familiar location.
stories.why_it_matters: This signals a shift toward standardized, transparent data governance in AI development—moving away from the practice of training on all available web content by default. For your teaching work, it's a concrete example of responsible AI in practice and how compliance needs can drive industry coordination. As someone building AI expertise, understanding the data provenance and usage policies behind models is increasingly essential; this standard will become a governance consideration in how you advise clients about model choices and training practices.
stories.potential_use: Use this in AI education to discuss the tension between model performance (which benefits from diverse training data) and creator rights and consent. In consulting, this is relevant when advising clients on their own content strategy—whether to opt out, what the trade-offs are, and how to document data governance decisions. It's also a useful framework for exploring India's emerging AI regulation and data sovereignty concerns with workshop participants.

sources.title: Making it easier for websites to express AI training preferences
